{{short description|Existence of antipodal pairs in covers of spheres}}
{{about|the theorem on covers of spheres|the theorem on simple closed geodesics on spheres|theorem of the three geodesics}}
[[File:Uniform tiling 332-t02.svg|thumb|A two-dimensional sphere '''S'''<sup>2</sup> covered by three closed sets, the closures of the red, yellow, and blue areas, in the pattern of a [[cuboctahedron]]. The red and yellow sets do not contain any antipodal pairs (each red or yellow triangle is opposite a triangle of the other color), but the center of each blue quadrilateral is antipodal to another blue quadrilateral.]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''Lusternik–Schnirelmann theorem''', aka '''Lusternik–Schnirelmann–Borsuk theorem''' or '''LSB theorem''' gives a [[sufficient condition]] for the inclusion of [[antipodal point]]s in a [[Cover (topology)|cover]] of a [[sphere]].

It is named after [[Lazar Lyusternik]] and [[Lev Schnirelmann]], who published it in 1930.<ref>{{citation
 | last  = Bollobás | first = Béla |authorlink= Béla Bollobás
 | doi   = 10.1017/CBO9780511816574

 | pages = 118–119
 | publisher = [[Cambridge University Press]]|location= New York
 | title     = The art of mathematics: Coffee time in Memphis
 | url       = https://books.google.com/books?id=ButlynVk25MC&pg=PA118
 | year      = 2006}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|first1=Lazar|last1=Lusternik|author1-link=Lazar Lyusternik|first2=Lev|last2=Schnirelmann|author2-link=Lev Schnirelmann|title=Méthodes topologiques dans les problèmes variationnels|publisher=Gosudarstvennoe Izdat.|location=Moscow|year=1930}}. {{harvtxt|Bollobás|2006}} cites pp. 26–31 of this 68-page pamphlet for the theorem.</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://projecteuclid.org/download/pdf_1/euclid.jgsp/1495850562 |title=Applications of Lusternik–Schnirelmann theorem Category and its Generalizations, John Oprea, Communicated by Vasil V. Tsanov, on Journal of Geometry and Symmetry in Physics ISSN 1312-5192}}</ref>

==Statement==
The sphere or [[hypersphere]] <math>S^n</math> is an <math>n</math>-dimensional surface, conventionally embedded as the set of [[unit vector]]s in the <math>(n+1)</math>-dimensional space <math>\mathbb{R}^{n+1}</math>. In this embedding, the pairs of unit vectors <math>(x,-x)</math> are antipodal (polar opposites). A cover is a family of subsets of the sphere whose union is the entire sphere. Intuitively, a subset of the sphere is a [[closed set]] if it includes all of its boundary points, or more formally if it contains all [[Limit (mathematics)|limits of sequences]] of points in the subset. The Lusternik–Schnirelmann theorem can then be stated as:
{{Math theorem |name=Lusternik–Schnirelmann theorem |If the sphere <math>S^n</math> is covered by <math>n+1</math> closed sets, then at least one of these sets contains a pair of antipodal points.}}

The related  [[Lusternik–Schnirelmann category]] of a topological space is the minimum number of subsets in a cover for which each subset is topologically simple (in a technical sense). It is at most two for a sphere, which can be covered by two [[Hemisphere (geometry)|hemispheres]]. However, the sphere can be used to construct a more complicated [[projective space]] <math>\mathbb{RP}^n</math>, the [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient space]] obtained by treating each pair of antipodal points as a single point. The Lusternik–Schnirelmann theorem implies that the Lusternik–Schnirelmann category of <math>\mathbb{RP}^n</math> is at least <math>n+1</math>, and it turns out to equal <math>n+1</math>.

== Proof ==

The theorem can be proved by leveraging the relationship between <math>S^n</math> and <math>\mathbb{RP}^n</math>, and the Borsuk-Ulam theorem in higher dimensions.<ref>{{Citation|isbn=0-521-79540-0|title=Algebraic Topology|last1=Hatcher|first1=Allen|author-link=Allen Hatcher|year=2002|url=https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch1.pdf|publisher=Cambridge University Press|page=33|quote=Assuming the higher-dimensional version of the Borsuk-Ulam theorem, the same arguments show that <math>S^n</math> cannot be covered by <math>n+1</math> closed sets without antipodal pairs of points, though it can be covered by <math>n+2</math> such sets, as the higher-dimensional analog of a tetrahedron shows.|section=Section 1.1}}</ref>

Real Projective Space <math>\mathbb{RP}^n</math> is defined as the quotient space of <math>S^n</math> by the antipodal map, where each point <math>x \in S^n</math> is identified with its antipodal point <math>-x \in S^n</math>. In other words, <math>\mathbb{RP}^n = S^n / \sim</math>, where <math>x \sim -x</math>. 

A pair of antipodal points in <math>S^n</math> corresponds to a single point in <math>\mathbb{RP}^n</math>. The concept of "containing a pair of antipodal points" in a subset of <math>S^n</math> is equivalent to that subset having a non-empty intersection with the pre-image of some point in <math>\mathbb{RP}^n</math> under the projection map <math>\pi: S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n</math>. 

The [[Borsuk-Ulam theorem]] states that for any continuous map <math>f: S^n \to \mathbb{R}^n</math>, there exists at least one pair of antipodal points <math>\{x, -x\}</math> in <math>S^n</math> such that <math>f(x) = f(-x)</math>.

Consider <math>S^n</math> expressed as the union of <math>n+1</math> closed sets <math>A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_{n+1}</math>. 

Define distance functions <math>d_i(x) = \inf_{y \in A_i} |x-y|</math> for <math>i=1, \ldots, n</math>. These are continuous functions. 

Construct a map <math>F: S^n \to \mathbb{R}^n</math> given by <math>F(x) = (d_1(x), d_2(x), \ldots, d_n(x))</math>. 

By the Borsuk-Ulam theorem, there exists a pair of antipodal points <math>\{x_0, -x_0\}</math> such that <math>F(x_0) = F(-x_0)</math>, meaning <math>d_i(x_0) = d_i(-x_0)</math> for all <math>i=1, \ldots, n</math>. 

If any <math>d_i(x_0) = 0</math>, then <math>x_0 \in A_i</math>. Since <math>d_i(x_0) = d_i(-x_0) = 0</math>, then <math>-x_0 \in A_i</math> as well (because <math>A_i</math> is closed). Thus, <math>A_i</math> contains a pair of antipodal points. 

If <math>d_i(x_0) > 0</math> for all <math>i=1, \ldots, n</math>, then <math>x_0 \notin A_i</math> for <math>i=1, \ldots, n</math>. Since <math>S^n = \bigcup_{j=1}^{n+1} A_j</math>, it must be that <math>x_0 \in A_{n+1}</math>. Similarly, since <math>d_i(-x_0) > 0</math> for all <math>i=1, \ldots, n</math>, then <math>-x_0 \notin A_i</math> for <math>i=1, \ldots, n</math>, implying <math>-x_0 \in A_{n+1}</math>. Therefore, <math>A_{n+1}</math> contains a pair of antipodal points.
